elements.id-string-3: In the last year alone, a surge of new benchmarks to measure \textit{compositional} understanding of vision-language models have permeated the machine learning ecosystem.Given an image, these benchmarks probe a model's ability to identify its associated caption amongst a set of compositional distractors.Surprisingly, we find significant biases in \textit{all} these benchmarks rendering them hackable.
elements.id-string-4: This hackability is so dire that blind models with no access to the image outperform state-of-the-art vision-language models.To remedy this rampant vulnerability, we introduce \method, a new benchmark for vision-language compositionality evaluation.We employ large language models, instead of rule-based templates used in previous benchmarks, to generate fluent and sensical hard negatives, and utilize an adversarial refinement mechanism to maximally reduce biases.
elements.id-string-5: We re-evaluate state-of-the-art models and recently proposed compositionality inducing strategies, and find that their improvements were hugely overestimated, suggesting that more innovation is needed in this important direction.
elements.id-string-6: We release \method and the code for evaluation at: \url{https://github.com/RAIVNLab/sugar-crepe}.
elements.id-string-8: Scholars today herald \emph{compositionality} as a fundamental presupposition characterizing both human perception and linguistic processing~\cite{cresswell1973logics}.
elements.id-string-9: Through compositional reasoning, humans can comprehend new scenes and describe those scenes by composing known atoms~\cite{janssen1997compositionality,hupkes2020compositionality,bottou2014machine,chomsky1965some}.
elements.id-string-10: For instance, compositionality allows people to differentiate between a photo of ``a girl in white facing a man in black'' and ``a girl in black facing a man in white''.
elements.id-string-11: For a while now, vision-language research has sought to develop models that can similarly comprehend scenes and express them through compositional language~\cite{krishna2017visual,ji2020action,lu2016visual,GrundeMcLaughlin2021AGQA}.
elements.id-string-12: Given its importance, a surge of new benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate whether vision-language models exhibit compositionality.
elements.id-string-13: Recently,  Winoground~\cite{thrush2022winoground}, VL-CheckList~\cite{zhao2022vl}, ARO~\cite{yuksekgonul2023when}, CREPE~\cite{ma2022crepe}, and Cola~\cite{ray2023cola} have entered the machine learning zeitgeist.
elements.id-string-14: Evaluation is mostly done through an image-to-text retrieval task formulation: by measuring how often models pick the description, ``a girl in white facing a man in black'' when presented with an image of it, and avoid choosing the incorrect \emph{hard negative} description, ``a girl in black facing a man in white''.
elements.id-string-15: In this work, we uncover a crucial vulnerability in not just one but all these image-to-text compositionality benchmarks:
elements.id-string-16: We find that a \emph{blind} model that never looks at the image, can identify the correct caption and avoid choosing the supposed ``hard negatives''.
elements.id-string-17: This blind model outperforms a wide array of pretrained vision-language models across the suite of benchmarks~\cite{RadfordKHRGASAM21,ilharco_gabriel_2021_5143773,gadre2023datacomp}.
elements.id-string-18: We explain this undesired hackability in existing benchmarks by showcasing that there exists a significant distributional gap between the positive and hard negative captions.
elements.id-string-19: For instance, in the ARO benchmark~\cite{yuksekgonul2023when}, human-generated positive captions differ drastically from the hard negative texts generated by randomly shuffling words in the positive captions.
elements.id-string-20: As new research has begun to propose methods that claim to improve compositionality on these benchmarks~\cite{yuksekgonul2023when,ray2023cola}, we find it critical to highlight our findings and propose a solution.
elements.id-string-21: We propose a solution to existing hackable benchmarks by introducing \method, a new benchmark to faithfully evaluate compositionality.
elements.id-string-22: In curating \method, we identify two main \emph{biases}~\footnote{\ We use biases and artifacts interchangeably in the paper.} that result in the distributional gap between positive and hard negatives; and employ mechanisms to fix the shifts.
elements.id-string-23: In particular, we find the current procedure in generating hard negatives introduces descriptions that are (1) not plausible and (2) non-fluent.
elements.id-string-24: For example, while the caption ``olives and grapes on a plate'' is a sensical fluent caption, benchmarks often have non-plausible hard negatives like ``olives and grapes inside a plate'' or simply incomprehensible ones like ``right has word another word.
elements.id-string-25: There is a words'' (see Table~\ref{tab:bad_hn_examples} for more examples).
elements.id-string-26: We mitigate such biases by first leveraging a modern large language model, ChatGPT~\cite{chatgpt}, to generate plausible and natural hard negative texts instead of relying on simple rule-based templates employed by existing benchmarks~\cite{ma2022crepe,yuksekgonul2023when}.
elements.id-string-27: Then, we subsample the dataset through an adversarial refinement process to ensure the identified biases are maximally removed by drawing on recent dataset de-biasing work~\cite{zellers2018swag,sakaguchi2021winogrande,le2020adversarial}.
elements.id-string-28: Taken together, this workflow is where \method derived its name: \textbf{S}ynthetic yet \textbf{U}nbiased \textbf{G}eneration with \textbf{A}dversarially \textbf{R}efined \textbf{C}ompositional \textbf{REP}resentation \textbf{E}valuation.
elements.id-string-29: We qualitatively and quantitatively verify through both human and automatic evaluations that \method\ effectively fixes these biases.
elements.id-string-30: With \method, we \emph{re}-evaluate recent methods proposed to improve compositionality.
elements.id-string-31: Specifically, we focus on one prominent approach that aims to improve compositionality through data augmentation.
elements.id-string-32: This method trains models by generating compositional hard negatives and injecting them within a training batch~\cite{doveh2023teaching,yuksekgonul2023when}.
elements.id-string-33: Unfortunately, we observe that the effectiveness of this simple data augmentation approach is hugely \emph{overestimated} when evaluated on existing benchmarks, leading to limited improvements on \method.
elements.id-string-34: Finally, we evaluate a wide variety of $17$ pretrained CLIP models~\cite{RadfordKHRGASAM21,ilharco_gabriel_2021_5143773,gadre2023datacomp}, and find that current models still lack compositionality.
elements.id-string-35: Our results suggest that to improve compositionality, future work may need more innovative techniques.
elements.id-string-37: We situate our paper amongst existing work on vision-language compositionality, and debiasing datasets for model evaluation.
elements.id-string-39: Recent works have introduced benchmarks to evaluate the compositionality of vision-language models~\cite{RadfordKHRGASAM21}; they find that current models exhibit little compositional understanding~\cite{yuksekgonul2023when,thrush2022winoground,zhao2022vl, ma2022crepe, ray2023cola} despite their remarkable performance on downstream tasks~\cite{RadfordKHRGASAM21, 0001LXH22, singh2022flava, alayrac2022flamingo, wang2022omnivl,wang2022image, zhai2022lit}.
elements.id-string-40: Models have a hard time discerning between text containing the same words ordered differently~\cite{thrush2022winoground}.
elements.id-string-41: Models also fail to link objects to their attributes, or understand the relationship between objects~\cite{zhao2022vl, yuksekgonul2023when, ray2023cola}.
elements.id-string-42: Our work finds that many of the benchmarks used to evaluate compositionality have hackable biases; blind models that do not even look at the image outperform state-of-the-art vision-language models.
elements.id-string-44: To enhance vision-language models’ compositionality, new proposals suggest training strategies that utilize additional data, models, and/or losses~\cite{yuksekgonul2023when, cascantebonilla2023going, ray2023cola, doveh2023teaching, Singh2023CoarsetoFineCL}.
elements.id-string-45: Amongst them, one prominent approach is to explicitly train the models to distinguish hard negatives from the correct captions~\cite{yuksekgonul2023when, doveh2023teaching}.
elements.id-string-46: While these approaches appear to improve compositionality on benchmarks, it is unclear if these models achieve such improvements by actually acquiring compositional understanding or by exploiting biases in these datasets.
elements.id-string-47: We answer this question in our evaluation.
elements.id-string-49: Several prior manuscripts have pointed out that biased datasets could lead to an overestimation of models' true capabilities~\cite{gururangan-etal-2018-annotation}.
elements.id-string-50: They have proposed dataset de-biasing methods to enable more faithful model evaluations~\cite{reif2023fighting,zellers2018swag,sakaguchi2021winogrande,le2020adversarial}.
elements.id-string-51: For instance, adversarial filtering~\cite{zellers2018swag} iteratively trains an ensemble of classifiers on different training splits and uses them to filter out ``easy'' negatives for each instance.
elements.id-string-52: Building upon adversarial filtering, AFLite~\cite{sakaguchi2021winogrande,le2020adversarial} filters data instances in a more light-weight manner without retraining a model at each iteration and leads to benchmarks that more accurately represent the underlying tasks.
elements.id-string-53: We use adversarial refinement to remove biases that creep into the generation of compositionality benchmarks.
elements.id-string-54: Current compositionality benchmarks and their biases
elements.id-string-55: A majority of existing compositionality benchmarks for vision-language models formulate the evaluation task as image-to-text retrieval~\cite{zhao2022vl,yuksekgonul2023when,ma2022crepe}.
elements.id-string-56: We focus on these benchmarks and discuss others~\cite{thrush2022winoground,ray2023cola} in Appendix~\ref{app:bms}.
elements.id-string-57: Given an image, the model is probed to select text that correctly describes the image from a pool of candidates.
elements.id-string-58: Unlike standard retrieval tasks where the negative (incorrect) candidates differ a lot from the \emph{positive} (correct) text, compositionality benchmarks intentionally design \emph{hard negative} texts that differ minimally from the positive text, in order to test whether the model understands the fine-grained atomic concepts that compose the scene.
elements.id-string-59: \textbf{Existing hard negative generation process introduces undesirable biases.}
elements.id-string-60: Existing benchmarks generate hard negative texts through rule-based programmatic procedures~\cite{zhao2022vl,yuksekgonul2023when,ma2022crepe}, which produce hard negatives by replacing a word of specific type (an object, attribute, or relation) in the original text, by swapping two words, or by shuffling the word order.
elements.id-string-61: We find that such procedures introduce unintentional biases in the generated hard negatives (see Table~\ref{tab:bad_hn_examples});
elements.id-string-62: specifically, we observe two major types of undesirable artifacts: (1) \emph{nonsensical} artifacts, and (2) \emph{non-fluent} artifacts.
elements.id-string-63: We then utilize Vera~\cite{liu2023vera}, a plausibility estimation model, to characterize the nonsensical bias.
elements.id-string-64: To capture the non-fluent bias, we leverage a grammar-check model~\cite{morris2020textattack} that assigns high scores to grammatically correct texts.
elements.id-string-65: We find that Vera and the grammar model assign higher scores to positive texts, suggesting that many hard negatives are nonsensical and not fluent (Figure~\ref{fig:vera_gap_existing}).

elements.id-string-91: We introduce \method, a new benchmark for faithful evaluation of vision-language models' compositionality based on the image-text pairs of COCO~\cite{lin2014microsoft}.
elements.id-string-92: \method presents two key contributions over existing benchmarks: (1) it drastically reduces the two identified dataset biases (Sec.~\ref{sec:data_generation}), and (2) it covers a broad range of fine-grained types of hard negatives (Sec.~\ref{sec:hn_types}).
elements.id-string-93: We present a summary comparison on compositionality benchmarks in Appendix~\ref{app:bms}.
elements.id-string-95: The generation procedure of \method consists of three main stages, centered around creating sensical and fluent hard negatives that close the distributional gaps to the positive texts, and ensuring a balanced distribution on the score gaps to make the final dataset robust to the identified biases.
elements.id-string-96: \textbf{Stage 1: Generate sensical and fluent hard negatives with a large language model.}
elements.id-string-97: Observing the capability of modern large language models in generating fluent and plausible texts, we leverage ChatGPT~\cite{chatgpt} to generate hard negative texts where we explicitly instruct it to avoid commonsense (logical) and fluency (grammatical) errors.
elements.id-string-98: To guide ChatGPT in re-writing a given positive text into its hard negative counterparts, we provide few-shot demonstrations written by the authors and leverage its in-context learning ability to generalize to unseen texts.
elements.id-string-99: Figure~\ref{fig:example_prompt} shows an example demonstration used and an actual hard negative generated.
elements.id-string-100: We detail all the prompt templates in Appendix~\ref{app:prompt}.
elements.id-string-101: Table~\ref{tab:sugar_crepe_examples} shows the comparisons between hard negatives generated from ChatGPT in \method and that from existing benchmarks.
elements.id-string-102: \textbf{Stage 2: Filter false negatives with human validation.}
elements.id-string-103: A generated text is considered a valid hard negative only if it incorrectly describes the corresponding image.
elements.id-string-104: For example, given an image with a positive caption ``a man and a child sitting on a sofa'', a compositional change that replaces ``child'' with ``girl'' may still result in a correct caption.
elements.id-string-105: To ensure the validity of the hard negatives in \method, we filter out \textit{false} negatives by manually examining the generated hard negatives and their corresponding images.
elements.id-string-106: \begin{figure}  \begin{minipage}{0.52\textwidth}  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{imgs/sugar-crepe-prompt.pdf} \caption{Example prompt (black) and actual hard negative (green) generated from  ChatGPT.}  \end{minipage}\hfill \begin{minipage}{0.46\textwidth} \vspace{-3mm} \begin{algorithm}[H]  \small \caption{Adversarial Refinement}  \begin{algorithmic}[1] \Require Text-only model $M_1$ and $M_2$; Number of grids $K$; A set of candidates $\mathcal{D}=\left\{I_i, T^{\mathrm{p}}_i, T^{\mathrm{n}}_i\right\}_{i\in [N]}$, where $I_i$, $T^{\mathrm{p}}_i$, and $T^{\mathrm{n}}_i$ are $i$-th image, positive caption, and negative caption. \Ensure A subset $\bar{\mathcal{D}}\subset\mathcal{D}$ \State Calculate the model score gap for each candidate $g^{(1)}_i=M_1(T^\mathrm{p}_i)-M_1(T^\mathrm{n}_i)$ and $g^{(2)}_i=M_2(T^\mathrm{p}_i)-M_2(T^\mathrm{n}_i)$ \State Split the 2D space $[-1, 1]\times[-1, 1]$ to $K\times K$ equal-size grids. \State Place each candidate to a grid based on the score gaps $g^{(1)}_i$ and $g^{(2)}_i$. \State Initialize $\bar{\mathcal{D}}=\{\}$ \For{each pair of grid $(G_j, G^{*}_j)$ symmetric about the original point $(0, 0)$} \If{$|G_j| > |G^*_j|$} \State Sample $|G^*_j|$ candidates from $G_j$ and put them to $\bar{\mathcal{D}}$. \State Put candidates in $G^*_j$ to $\bar{\mathcal{D}}$. \Else \State Sample $|G_j|$ candidates from $G^*_j$ and put them to $\bar{\mathcal{D}}$. \State Put candidates in $G_j$ to $\bar{\mathcal{D}}$. \EndIf \EndFor \end{algorithmic}  \end{algorithm} \end{minipage} \vspace{-2ex} \end{figure}
elements.id-string-108: While ChatGPT yields more sensical and fluent text, there is no guarantee that the bias between positive and negative texts is negligible.
elements.id-string-109: Following dataset de-biasing work~\cite{zellers2018swag,sakaguchi2021winogrande,le2020adversarial}, we develop an adversarial refinement mechanism that maximally reduces the undesirably exploitable artifacts in \method.
elements.id-string-110: Specifically, our goal is to ensure that performance improvements on \method cannot be achieved by exploiting the identified nonsensical and non-fluent biases.
elements.id-string-111: To accomplish this, we characterize the biases again with the commonsense and grammar models~\cite{liu2023vera,morris2020textattack}, and subsample the dataset to ensure symmetric score gap distributions on both the positive and negative sides, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:vera_gap_ours}.
elements.id-string-112: We note the symmetry around zero implies that the commonsense and grammar scores can no longer be used to infer the ground truth positive texts.

elements.id-string-114: \method covers a broad range of hard negative types
elements.id-string-115: To test different aspects of vision-language models' compositional understanding, we follow CREPE~\cite{ma2022crepe} to consider various \emph{forms} of hard negatives, and follow VL-CheckList~\cite{zhao2022vl} and ARO~\cite{yuksekgonul2023when} to consider different fine-grained \emph{categories} of the atomic concepts.
elements.id-string-116: In total, \method covers $7$ fine-grained types of hard negatives, as shown in Table~\ref{tab:dataset_summary}.
elements.id-string-117: We introduce the dataset taxonomy below, starting from the \emph{form} of the hard negatives to its different \emph{finer-grained} variants.
elements.id-string-119: Given a positive text describing a scene, we generate a \replace\ hard negative by replacing an atomic concept in the original text with a new concept that makes the text mismatch with the original scene.
elements.id-string-120: Based on the type of the atomic concept---object, attribute, or relation---we further categorize \replace\ hard negatives into \replaceobj, \replaceatt, and \replacerel.
elements.id-string-121: \textbf{The \swap\ form.} Different from \replace, \swap\ does not introduce new concepts in the hard negatives, but a \swap\ hard negative is generated by swapping two atomic concepts of the same category in the positive text.
elements.id-string-122: We further categorize \swap\ into \swapobj\ and \swapatt, and omit swapping two relationships since it generally results in nonsensical texts.
elements.id-string-123: \textbf{The \add\ form.} Similar to the \replace\ form, but instead of replacing an atomic concept with a new one, we generate an \add\ hard negative by adding a new atomic concept to the positive text that makes it mismatch with the original scene.
elements.id-string-124: We only further categorize \add\ into \addobj~(adding object concept) and \addatt~(adding attribute concept), as adding new relationship concepts to the positive texts often make them highly implausible.
elements.id-string-125: \textbf{Dataset overview.} The final evaluation set of \method consists of $7512$ examples, where the numbers for each fine-grained type are listed in Table~\ref{tab:dataset_summary}.
elements.id-string-126: Each example is an image-to-text retrieval task composed of an image, a positive text, and a hard negative.
elements.id-string-127: On \method, random chance performance has an average accuracy of $50\%$.
elements.id-string-128: We note that ARO and CREPE additionally consider \shuffle\ (randomly shuffling words in a sentence) and \negate\ (adding negation keywords ``no/not'' to a sentence) hard negatives.
elements.id-string-129: We however omit them in \method as \shuffle\ is very unlikely to be plausible and fluent, and \negate\ introduces irreducible keyword artifacts~\cite{ma2022crepe}.~\footnote{One can easily infer hard negatives from whether the text contains negation keywords ``no/not''.}

elements.id-string-177: Re-evaluating recent methods for improving compositionality
elements.id-string-178: Given the vulnerability of existing compositionality benchmarks, it is unclear whether recently proposed methods that show state-of-the-art performances on these benchmarks are indeed effective.
elements.id-string-179: Thus, we re-evaluate these methods with \method.
elements.id-string-181: Specifically, we focus on evaluating one common \emph{data-augmentation} approach considered in~\cite{yuksekgonul2023when,doveh2023teaching}, where the core idea is to explicitly create hard negatives and train the model to distinguish them.
elements.id-string-182: We broadly refer to this training scheme as \negclip following \cite{yuksekgonul2023when}.
elements.id-string-183: We evaluate two \negclip training schemes: finetuning and training from scratch.
elements.id-string-184: For finetuning, in addition to taking the model released in \cite{yuksekgonul2023when}, we finetune another three \negclip\ models (using ViT-B/32 following~\cite{yuksekgonul2023when}) with three respective types of hard negatives (\ie, \replace, \swap, \negate) generated using CREPE's~\cite{ma2022crepe} source code.
elements.id-string-185: For training from scratch, we use RN50 as the base model and train variants of \negclip by augmenting the training examples with different types of hard negatives.
elements.id-string-186: We perform both training and finetuning on COCO~\cite{lin2014microsoft}.
elements.id-string-187: \textbf{Improvements are overestimated due to unintentionally overfitting.}
elements.id-string-188: In Table~\ref{tab:re_eval}, we first see that \negclip\ finetuned models show significant improvements on \hncoco, boosting the performance more than 10\% compared to standard CLIP finetuning on 11 out of 16 cases (highlighted in green).
elements.id-string-189: The lifts are especially large when the hard negative type used in finetuning matches that used in evaluation, where \negclip\ finetuned models can achieve near human-level performances.
elements.id-string-190: For instance, by finetuning with \replace\ hard negatives, \negclip\ reaches 94\% on \hncoco\ evaluated with \replace\ hard negatives (human performance is 95\%).
elements.id-string-191: While the results on \hncoco\ suggest that \negclip\ is seemingly sufficient in equipping models with strong compositionality, we however see that the improvements brought by \negclip\ are much smaller on \method.
elements.id-string-192: In fact, none of the improvements on \method is larger than 10\%, and the best performing \negclip\ finetuned models still have large gaps to human-level performances, \eg, best \negclip\ model lags behind human by 23\% on \method's \swap\ hard negatives.
elements.id-string-193: Similarly, when trained from scratch, we observe the same trend that \negclip's improvements are much larger on \hncoco\ than on \method.
elements.id-string-194: The improvements on \hncoco\ are again most pronounced when the training and testing hard negative type matches.
elements.id-string-195: We attribute the stark contrast in \negclip's effectiveness on \hncoco\ and \method to model's unintentional overfitting: The \negclip\ models learned to exploit artifacts that can be used to easily distinguish hard negatives from positives on \hncoco, instead of actually improving compositionality.
elements.id-string-196: Thus, when evaluated on \method where the artifacts are removed, the improvement from \negclip\ drastically reduces.
elements.id-string-197: These results imply that \negclip's effectiveness is overestimated on existing benchmarks, and we may still need further innovations to fundamentally improve a model's compositionality.
elements.id-string-198: \small\caption{Re-evaluating hard negative augmented training shows that the method's improvements on existing benchmarks (\hncoco) are hugely overestimated, particularly when the test hard negative type matches the one used in training, which can be attributed to overfitting the artifacts.Color notations: \colorbox{tablegreen}{Gains compared to standard CLIP (finetuned / from scratch) $>$ 10\%}.}
elements.id-string-202: Comprehensive evaluations on existing pretrained vision-language models
elements.id-string-203: \small\caption{Our evaluation of pretrained CLIP models on \method shows that they demonstrate compositionality on some hard negatives but are far from human performance on others, especially on \swap\ hard negatives or ones perturbing attributes and relations (also illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:imagenet_correlation}: lower overall performance on \swap, and lower performances on attributes/relations compared to objects).}\scalebox{0.6}{
elements.id-string-205: We present four key findings in our evaluation over $17$ pretrained CLIP models on \method, with results reported in Table~\ref{tab:eval_ours} and visualized in Figure~\ref{fig:imagenet_correlation}.
elements.id-string-206: \textbf{The best pretrained CLIP models demonstrate some compositional understanding but still have overall large rooms for improvements.} Table~\ref{tab:eval_ours} shows that the largest pretrained CLIP models, \eg, OpenAI's RN50x64, LAION's xlm-roberta-large-ViT-H-14, and DataComp's ViT-L-14, achieve near-human performance on \replaceobj.
elements.id-string-207: However, on \replaceobj, smaller models pretrained on small datasets still suffer from big drops in performance --- 23\% and 43\% respectively for DataComp's small and medium models --- compared to humans.
elements.id-string-208: Additionally, on nearly all other hard negative types, there are clear gaps (larger than 10\%) between the best model performances and human performances, showing an overall large room for improvements in current models' compositionality.
elements.id-string-209: \textbf{All models struggle at identifying \swap\ hard negatives, regardless of their pertaining dataset and model size.} Among the three types of hard negatives, \swap\ hard negatives present the biggest challenge to the pretrained CLIP models, even though humans can easily tell them apart from the positive captions.
elements.id-string-210: We observe in Table~\ref{tab:eval_ours} that all models demonstrate low performance on both \swapobj\ and \swapatt\ hard negatives regardless of their pretraining dataset and model sizes, with the difference from human performance reaching from 27\% to 50\%.
elements.id-string-211: \textbf{Existing models are object-centric, struggling to compose attributes and relations.} We find that existing pretrained models are a lot better at composing objects than attributes or relations (Table~\ref{tab:eval_ours}).
elements.id-string-212: This finding holds for both \replace\ and \add\ hard negatives but not the most difficult \swap\ negatives, where models perform equally poorly on both \swapobj\ and \swapatt.
elements.id-string-213: On \replace\ hard negatives, even though most models achieve human-level performance on \replaceobj, they all suffer from a drop in performance on \replaceatt\ and \replacerel, where the drop is as large as 15\% and 29\% respectively.
elements.id-string-214: Similarly, on \add\ hard negatives, all models except for DataComp's small:ViT-B-32 experience a decrease in performance from \addobj\ to \addatt, with the largest difference reaching 10\%.
elements.id-string-215: \textbf{Models' performance on \method correlates with their ImageNet zero-shot accuracy.}
elements.id-string-216: \begin{figure}[t]  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{imgs/imagenet_zeroshot_correlation.png} \caption{We plot pretrained vision-language models' zero-shot top-1 accuracy on ImageNet versus their retrieval recall@1 on \method, where $r$ is the Pearson correlation coefficient. This plot suggests that models' ImageNet zero-shot accuracy positively correlates with their compositionality.}  \end{figure}
elements.id-string-217: We show in Figure~\ref{fig:imagenet_correlation} that there is a positive correlation between models' performance on \method and their zero-shot accuracy on ImageNet.
elements.id-string-218: This correlation is moderate on \swapobj\ and \addatt\ (Pearson correlation coefficient $r = 0.78$ and $r = 0.75$ respectively) and strong on all other hard negatives ($r > 0.8$).
elements.id-string-220: Our investigation reveals significant biases present in existing benchmarks for the compositional comprehension capability of vision-language models.
elements.id-string-221: The severity of this vulnerability is exemplified by text-only models without access to the image outperforming vision-language models.
elements.id-string-222: To address this, we introduce \method, a novel benchmark for evaluating the compositionality of vision-language understanding.
elements.id-string-223: Unlike previous benchmarks that relied on rule-based templates, we leverage large language models to generate less biased negatives and employ adversarial filtering mechanisms to minimize biases.
elements.id-string-224: Through reassessment of state-of-the-art models and recently proposed compositionality inducing mechanisms, we uncover a significant overestimation of their advancements, underscoring the need for further innovation.
elements.id-string-227: Limitation, future work, and societal impact
elements.id-string-229: There are several limitations to this work that future research can further explore.
elements.id-string-230: First, we focus our scope on compositionality benchmarks formulated as image-to-text retrieval task.
elements.id-string-231: While this is currently the most prevailing evaluation framework, future research can characterize compositionality evaluation as text-to-image retrieval problem, as in the initial efforts considered by~\cite{ray2023cola,thrush2022winoground}.
elements.id-string-232: More importantly, we hope our work can guide future efforts in creating and ensuring faithful compositionality benchmarks in text-to-image form.
elements.id-string-233: Second, in this work, we identify \emph{two} human interpretable dataset biases, the nonsensical and non-fluent biases, which may not cover all dataset artifacts that could possibly be exploited by a model.
elements.id-string-234: Future work may utilize more sophisticated techniques to remove spurious dataset artifacts beyond human comprehension~\cite{le2020adversarial}.
elements.id-string-235: Finally, we focus our evaluations on contrastively learned vision-language models~\cite{RadfordKHRGASAM21}.
elements.id-string-236: Future work should include and characterize the compositionality of modern generative vision-language models~\cite{alayrac2022flamingo,chen2022pali,li2023blip2,tschannen2023image}.
elements.id-string-238: As vision-language models such as CLIP~\cite{RadfordKHRGASAM21} are becoming the foundation models for many downstream applications~\cite{rombach2022high,ramesh2022hierarchical}, it is imperative to understand the limitations of these models to avoid misuses and undesirable outcomes~\cite{cho2022dall,bianchi2022easily}.
elements.id-string-239: Compositionality benchmarks probe a model's understanding of finer-grained concepts, and hence allow us to identify blind spots~\cite{yuksekgonul2023when,zhao2022vl,ma2022crepe} of seemingly powerful models deemed by standard classification and retrieval benchmarks~\cite{Deng2009ImageNetAL,lin2014microsoft}.
elements.id-string-240: Our work further alleviates common artifacts in existing compositionality benchmarks that result in overestimation of a model's capability.
elements.id-string-241: We hope our proposed benchmark \method leads to more faithful assessment of a vision-language model's compositionality, and can hence guide more accurate usages of the models.
elements.id-string-242: Nevertheless, we note that strong performances on \method do not imply perfect models.
elements.id-string-243: We envision \method being one of the many benchmarks used to comprehensively understand the abilities of vision-language models from various aspects.

elements.id-string-262: We provide an overview of existing vision-language compositionality benchmarks below, with Table~\ref{tab:benchmark_comp} summarizing the dataset comparisons.
elements.id-string-264: A majority of current benchmarks formulate the evaluation task as image-to-text retrieval problem.
elements.id-string-265: These benchmarks generate hard negative texts procedurally through rule-based templates, where each benchmark considers different types of hard negatives.
elements.id-string-266: \textbf{VL-Checklist~\cite{zhao2022vl}.} VL-CheckList aims at evaluating vision-language models' understanding of different objects, attributes, and relationships.
elements.id-string-267: It contains \replace\ hard negatives generated by replacing atomic parts of the positive texts with other foils.
elements.id-string-268: VL-CheckList further breaks the hard negatives down into more granular categories based on the type of the replaced atomic part, \ie, object, attribute, or relationship.
elements.id-string-269: \textbf{ARO~\cite{yuksekgonul2023when}.} ARO focuses on models' understanding of different relationships, attributes, and order information.
elements.id-string-271: \swap\ hard negatives are generated by swapping two words in the positive texts; on the other hand, \shuffle\ hard negatives are generated by shuffling words in the positive texts.
elements.id-string-272: ARO further divides \swap\ hard negatives into attribute or relationship type.
elements.id-string-273: \textbf{CREPE~\cite{ma2022crepe}.} CREPE is a large-scale evaluation benchmark that includes three types of hard negatives: \replace, \swap\ and \negate.
elements.id-string-274: \replace\ and \swap\ hard negatives are generated as in VL-CheckList and ARO.
elements.id-string-275: In addition, \negate\ hard negatives are generated by adding negation keywords (\ie, \textit{not} or \textit{no}) to the original positive texts.
elements.id-string-276: The hard negatives are not further divided into fine-grained types (object, attribute, or relations).
elements.id-string-278: Complementary to image-to-text formulation, compositionality can as well be evaluated by probing a model to select an image that best matches a given text description, against other hard negative images as distractors.
elements.id-string-279: Unlike hard negative texts, hard negative images are more difficult to obtain and thus current text-to-image compositionality benchmarks are smaller at scale.
elements.id-string-280: \paragraph{Winoground~\cite{thrush2022winoground}.} Winoground is a small dataset manually curated by human annotators.
elements.id-string-281: Each example in the dataset contains two images and two matching captions, where both captions contain identical words that appear in different orders.
elements.id-string-282: Note that Winoground can be used for either image-to-text or text-to-image retrieval.
elements.id-string-283: While the original intention for Winoground is to evaluate vision-language compositionality, recent work~\cite{diwan2022winoground} has pointed out that solving the tasks in Winoground requires not just compositional vision-language understanding, but additionally a suite of other abilities such as commonsense reasoning, or distinguishing visually difficult images.
elements.id-string-284: \paragraph{Cola~\cite{ray2023cola}.} Cola tests a vision-language model's ability to select an image that correctly matches a given caption, against another distractor image with the same objects and attributes but in the wrong composition.
elements.id-string-285: The image pairs are mined from existing datasets.
elements.id-string-286: As a result, the final evaluation set is relatively small in size ($210$ examples in total).
elements.id-string-287: We deem text-to-image evaluation as important as image-to-text evaluation.
elements.id-string-288: Future work can explore approaches to generate or mine compositional hard negative images at scale, as preliminarily explored in \cite{ray2023cola,yuksekgonul2023when}.

elements.id-string-302: Hard negative generation procedure and templates
elements.id-string-303: To generate hard negatives in \method, we come up with three different prompt templates for the three hard negative types considered: \replace, \swap, and \add.
elements.id-string-304: Each template consists of task instruction for generating the corresponding type of hard negatives and several ($7$ or more) few-shot demonstrations.
elements.id-string-305: We describe the general generation procedure and example prompt templates below and refer readers to our dataset repository for the full prompts used~\footnote{\url{https://github.com/RAIVNLab/sugar-crepe}} .
elements.id-string-306: \begin{figure}[t]  \begin{subfigure}{.4\textwidth}  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{imgs/prompt-replace-obj.pdf} \caption{\replaceobj.} \end{subfigure} \begin{subfigure}{.4\textwidth}  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{imgs/prompt-replace-att.pdf} \caption{\replaceatt.} \end{subfigure} \begin{subfigure}{.4\textwidth}  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{imgs/prompt-replace-rel.pdf} \caption{\replacerel.} \end{subfigure} \caption{Example prompt templates (black) and outputs (green) from ChatGPT for \replace\ hard negatives.}  \end{figure}

elements.id-string-310: To best leverage ChatGPT's capabilities, we devise a three-step workflow to generate \replace\ hard negatives: (1) We prompt ChatGPT in locating the desired atomic concepts (\eg, objects) in the sentence; (2) We prompt ChatGPT to generate a new concept to replace a randomly selected old concept; (3) We let ChatGPT compose a new sentence by replacing the old concept with the new one.
elements.id-string-311: For steps (1) and (3), we prompt ChatGPT with a temperature of $0.0$ to get stable outputs.
elements.id-string-312: For step (2), however, we diversify the outputs by prompting ChatGPT with a higher temperature of $1.5$.
elements.id-string-313: With this design, we are able to generate diverse \replace\ hard negatives.
elements.id-string-314: Figure~\ref{fig:prompt-replace} shows the example templates and outputs for \replace\ hard negatives.
elements.id-string-315: \textbf{Generating \swap\ hard negatives.} To generate \textsc{swap} hard negatives, which do not require any new concepts, we simply prompt ChatGPT once with a temperature of 0.0.
elements.id-string-316: Unlike \replace, \swap\ hard negatives are only possible when there are at least two atomic concepts of the same category, \ie, either object or attribute.
elements.id-string-317: Thus, our prompt first queries ChatGPT whether it is possible to swap two atomic concepts in the input sentence to generate a new description.
elements.id-string-318: Only if the answer is yes, will ChatGPT then proceed to identify two swappable concepts and compose the corresponding new sentence by swapping the two concepts.
elements.id-string-319: Figure~\ref{fig:prompt-swap} shows the example templates and outputs for \swap\ hard negatives.
elements.id-string-320: \textbf{Generating \add\ hard negatives.} Similar to the \replace, we also employ a three-step prompting procedure to generate \add\ hard negatives.
elements.id-string-321: The only difference in the procedure is that we prompt ChatGPT to add the generated new concept to the original caption, instead of using it to replace an old concept.
elements.id-string-322: Figure~\ref{fig:prompt-add} shows the example templates and outputs for \add\ hard negatives.
elements.id-string-324: We detail the adversarial refinement procedure below.
elements.id-string-325: Given a text model $M$, we denote its output score for the positive and negative caption of $i$-th image as $M(p_{i})$ and $M(n_{i})$.
elements.id-string-326: If $M(p_{i})>M(n_{i})$, then the model could identify the correct caption for the $i$-th image without referring to it.
elements.id-string-327: For a test set to be unattackable given the text model $M$, the expectation of $M$'s identifying the correct caption should be as close to random guess as possible; in particular, we hope that $E_{i}[M(p_{i})>M(n_{i})]=0.5$.
elements.id-string-328: To achieve this for both the grammar model $M_1$ and plausibility model $M_2$, we first calculate the score difference $g^{(1)}_i=M_{1}(p_{i})-M_{1}(n_{i})$ and  $g^{(2)}_i=M_{2}(p_{i})-M_{2}(n_{i})$, where the range of both $g^{(1)}$ and $g^{(2)}$ is $[-1, 1]$.
elements.id-string-329: Then we split the 2D space of the joint range of  $g^{(1)}$ and $g^{(2)}$ into $100\times 100$ equal grids, and for each pair of symmetric grids, \eg, $\{(g^{(1)}, g^{(2)})|g^{(1)}\in(0.02, 0.04], g^{(2)}\in(-0.04, 0.06]\}$ and $\{(g^{(1)}, g^{(2)})|g^{(1)}\in(-0.02, -0.04], g^{(2)}\in(0.04, -0.06]\}$, we preserve the same number of data for both grids, therefore we ensure that for the resultant set, $E_{i}[M_{1}(p_{i})>M_{1}(n_{i})]=0.5$ and $E_{i}[M_{2}(p_{i})>M_{2}(n_{i})]=0.5$.

elements.id-string-353: To compare the quality of the hard negatives generated in \method to those in current benchmarks (\ie, \hncoco), we randomly sample $100$ examples for each of the hard negative types: \replace, \swap, and \negate\ / \add.
elements.id-string-354: Each example is organized to consist of (1) the original positive text, (2) its hard negative in \hncoco, and (3) its hard negative in \method.
elements.id-string-355: For each example, a human user rates whether the hard negative in \hncoco\ or that in \method is better (or tie) in terms of commonsense and grammatical correctness, respectively.
elements.id-string-356: Note that we compare \negate\ in \hncoco\ to \add\ in \method, as both hard negatives are intended to probe a model's understanding of the \textit{existence or not} of an atomic concept.
